title: Editing and Maintaining Workflow Files
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of editing and maintaining workflow files and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to editing and maintaining workflow files.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on editing and maintaining workflow files. Workflow changes should be reviewed like source code: validate YAML/schema, understand trigger and permission changes, test on a low-risk branch, and review the run. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Editing and Maintaining Workflow Files matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Workflow changes should be reviewed like source code: validate YAML/schema, understand trigger and permission changes, test on a low-risk branch, and review the run. Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Workflow changes should be reviewed like source code: validate YAML/schema, understand trigger and permission changes, test on a low-risk branch, and review the run. Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Updating workflow definitions
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Reviewing workflow changes in pull requests
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Checking YAML indentation
items.text: YAML is indentation-sensitive. Check that nested values are aligned, values have the expected type, special strings are quoted when needed, and the workflow schema accepts the key at that level.

items.title: Naming workflows and jobs clearly
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Validating configuration before merging
items.text: For validating configuration before merging, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
name: Validate workflow configuration
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Replace with a real validation command"
content_blocks.expected_output: A push or pull request starts a read-only job; replace the demonstration command with a check appropriate to the repository.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to editing and maintaining workflow files. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain editing and maintaining workflow files, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Create and inspect the first workflow in a repository before adding complexity.

content.task: Apply editing and maintaining workflow files to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Workflow changes should be reviewed like source code: validate YAML/schema, understand trigger and permission changes, test on a low-risk branch, and review the run.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Workflow changes should be reviewed like source code: validate YAML/schema, understand trigger and permission changes, test on a low-risk branch, and review the run. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Workflow changes should be reviewed like source code: validate YAML/schema, understand trigger and permission changes, test on a low-risk branch, and review the run.
Keep workflow files in `.github/workflows/`, name jobs and steps clearly, and verify a committed change from the Actions run page rather than assuming a saved YAML file executed.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
